plan.concept: Shannon's discrete entropy H = -Σ p_i log p_i as a measure of choice/uncertainty, computed in bits for a small distribution.
learning_outcomes: Compute H for a small distribution and read it in bits.
See that certainty (one p_i = 1) gives H = 0 and n equally likely outcomes give log2 n bits.
See how each outcome's contribution -p_i log2 p_i adds up, and that zero-probability outcomes contribute 0.
plan.visual_strategy: Pipeline of probabilities -> contributions -> total; bars for p_i and contributions; sweep of H vs one probability; readout of key values.
plan.misconception: Entropy is not the number of outcomes; it is the average surprisal, so 4 equally likely outcomes give 2 bits but a skewed 4-outcome distribution gives less.

title: Shannon Entropy: Measuring Choice and Uncertainty in Bits
idea: Shannon asks for a number H(p_1,...,p_n) that measures how much choice or uncertainty a set of probabilities contains. He requires continuity, monotonic growth with n when outcomes are equally likely, and consistency when a choice is split into successive choices. Theorem 2 shows the only such measure is H = -K Σ p_i log p_i; with K = 1 and base-2 logs, H is measured in bits.
why_it_matters: H is the fundamental limit on how much a source can be compressed and how much information a symbol carries. It also gives a precise meaning to 'uncertainty': certainty gives 0 bits, and n equally likely outcomes give log2 n bits.

equations.caption: Theorem 2: the unique measure satisfying Shannon's three requirements; K sets the unit.
With K = 1 and base-2 logarithms, H is in bits.
The two-outcome case plotted in Fig. 7.

walkthrough: Choose n outcomes and assign each a raw weight w_i ≥ 0.
Normalize: p_i = w_i / Σ_j w_j, so the probabilities sum to 1.
For each outcome compute its surprisal -log2 p_i (0 if p_i = 0).
Weight by probability: contribution_i = -p_i log2 p_i.
Sum the contributions to get H = -Σ p_i log2 p_i bits.

explorations.title: Certainty gives zero bits
explorations.observe: H = 0 bits, and the contribution bars show one bar of 0 and two bars of 0.
explorations.why: One outcome has probability 1, so there is no choice; Shannon's property 1 says H = 0 exactly then.

explorations.title: Four equally likely outcomes give two bits
explorations.change: Set n = 4 and make all weights equal.
explorations.observe: Each p_i = 0.25, each contribution is 0.5 bits, and H = 2 bits = log2 4.
explorations.why: Property 2: with n equally likely outcomes H is maximal and equals log2 n.

misconception.title: Common misunderstanding
misconception.text: Entropy is not simply the number of outcomes. Four outcomes with probabilities 0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1 give H ≈ 1.36 bits, well below log2 4 = 2 bits, because the outcome is usually predictable.

checks.name: Four equally likely outcomes give 2 bits

from_paper: Theorem 2: the only H satisfying Shannon's three requirements is H = -K Σ p_i log p_i (Section 6).
Property 1: H = 0 if and only if all p_i but one are zero, that one being unity (Section 6).
Property 2: for a given n, H is maximum and equal to log n when all p_i are equal (Section 6).
With base-2 logarithms, H represents bits per symbol (Section 7).
our_simplifications: We use n between 2 and 4 and raw weights normalized to probabilities, rather than arbitrary distributions.
We set K = 1 and use base-2 logarithms so H is in bits.
The sweep varies only w_1 while the other weights stay fixed.
quotes: Quantities of the form H = -Σ p_i log p_i (the constant K merely amounts to a choice of a unit of measure) play a central role in information theory as measures of information, choice and uncertainty.
Thus only when we are certain of the outcome does H vanish. Otherwise H is positive.
